utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need closed session for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The evidence will continue in a moment when the noise stops. I have to remind you before we start that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you took at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, K88. I just have a few questions for you this morning. In 2001 did you provide an interview to a MUP working group that was tasked with investigating the discovery of a refrigerator truck in the Danube?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an interview, but it was rather informal and with my immediate superior. He asked me to go to the headquarters and tell them what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you later accompany members of the working group to the site that was depicted in the map we were looking at yesterday and show them the location of the grave-sites?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will follow the following order: Mr. -- General Lukic, Mr. Sainovic, General Lazarevic, General Pavkovic, General Ojdanic, and Mr. Milutinovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness K88. I apologise for having to address you that way, but it is for your protection, and hence I need to use the pseudonym. My name is Branko Lukic, I appear here on behalf of General Sreten Lukic. I'll have a few questions which would rather be an attempt in clarifying a few things. I will -- I believe I will be brief and after me the colleagues that will follow will probably have some additional questions, although not too many. Do you have your statement in B/C/S before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go to paragraph 3. I wanted to ask you something regarding that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 it states the following: "The armoured mechanised brigade was responsible for providing security for sports and public events. We also worked in Kosovo and had two bases there, one in Prizren and one in Pristina. I went there several times to train others to operate various MUP vehicles." Concerning this, I wanted to ask you the following: You personally were stationed in Belgrade and not in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The thing discussed here was 1992/1993, the thing discussed in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, in 1998 and 1999 you were stationed in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go to paragraph 5 now. The commander of the Belgrade unit was Zoran Simovic, the commander in Novi Sad was Branimir Curcic and in Pristina Radomir Stalevic. I can't recall what the commanders were in terms of rank, but the police ranks did not matter, rather, their position or function. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I used the best words at the time, but in any case I don't know what their rank was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. This will take me to my next question. This pertains to 1998 and 1999 whereby you say that their position was more important than the rank. It also goes for that period; that's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to say that one could be a lieutenant-colonel but could hold such a position to have command over a colonel, depending what their position were -- was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was clear to us and -- but this was just to clarify it for the people who do not originate from that part of the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, where is the reference to the distinction between ranks and functions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph number 5, that's second-last sentence -- actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's missing from my copy, then, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English second-last sentence is: "The command of the SAJ is in Batajnica now and no longer in Kneza Milos Street, Belgrade, since this was bombed in 1999."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then the sentence is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that first sentence I've read -- the sentence I've just read, is it in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Then there's a missing English sentence. Could you read to us, please, what that missing sentence is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll read it in B/C/S. [Interpretation] "I can't recall" -- [In English] You stopped with "1999."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the following part is: [Interpretation] "The commander of the SAJ --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of the Belgrade unit was Zoran Simovic, commander of Novi Sad was Branimir Curcic, and commander of Pristina was Radomir Stalevic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've got that unit. That's not the one I'm concerned about. It's the one that says there was a difference between ranks and function.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm waiting for the transcript to pick up the names correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The following sentence is the next one. [Interpretation] "I cannot recall what the commanders were in terms of rank, but within the police rank was unimportant. What was important was the position occupied by the given person. Ranks were assigned depending on the number of years of professional experience and education."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this particular statement was actually in its original form in Serbian, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to clarify it with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This witness requested to sign his statement in the B/C/S, so it's been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you accept that this is an accurate reflection of a passage missing from paragraph 5?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was unaware that this passage was missing, this -- we had sent the translation to be revised earlier this week. I trust my colleague, if he says this passage appears in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Lukic, for clarifying that. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just want to emphasise that this page is signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness K88, in paragraph 8 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We should move to private session, Your Honour, because this is a paragraph where this witness can be identified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 11 of your statement. You say: "When the bombing started, the bombing of the VJ barracks next to us at the Batajnica base was hit by a NATO bomb and the doors and windows of our building were damaged. After that, once we moved out of the base, there was not any security at the main entrance. Basically anyone could come in and out at that time." You say "anyone could come in and out during that time," it includes the time-period where the trucks with the corpses appeared there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No one was there. One could approach it from all sides because the base was not secured, or rather, the security was very poor in physical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now go beyond the scope of the statement, but it concerns some additional information we received from the OTP. Is it correct that there were no attempts made to burn the bodies after they had been disposed of in the pit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am not dissatisfied with your answer; I'm waiting for the transcript. Therefore, do not think that I'm hesitating because of you. I wanted to ask you this: Is it also correct that while the pits were dug, there were tires placed around them and set alight so as to make a smoke-screen to prevent NATO aeroplanes from bombing the site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Someone must have told us that that would provide a degree of protection against NATO planes, and I think we set alight over 100 tires. We had technical difficulty in the sense that some of those tires fell into the pits and a facility was caught on fire nearby. There were lots of complications; however, on the other hand, every time we were digging, we would have to leave the site for a couple of hours on numerous occasions and then we would have to go back because of the air-raids.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question had to do with the tires, but you've already explained that and I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask to go back into private session yet again and this will be one last time because of the witness's security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday my colleague asked you, and also in paragraph 35 of your statement you said something about a man you described as a member of the DB, perhaps from Kosovo, perhaps not, who had a Montenegrin accent. My question is the following: Is it correct that were there are over 200.000 Montenegrins living in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So even if someone had a Montenegrin accent --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now my last question: Did you ever in any context hear that Sreten Lukic was in any way involved in this operation of transporting bodies from Kosovo to Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't even know about General Lukic at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness K88. I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, only a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. My name is Toma Fila, and I appear for the accused Sainovic. What I wanted to ask you is the following: My colleague Mr. Lukic asked you about the setting of tires on fire, but in paragraph 23 of your statement you said that you also set fire to petrol in order to get rid of the stench?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Some of the trucks had been standing there for a few days and things were dripping from the trucks so we used toilet cleaners. This was not successful, so we poured petrol on that and set it on fire. And the same applied to tires. It's hard to set a tire on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We are simply clarifying certain points as to why the tires were set on fire. My next question is the following: In several places in your statement you say one truck with bodies stood there for 15 days, another for so many days, and you've just mentioned that again. I see that you were a policeman for eight or nine years in logistics. Logistics requires good organisation. Would you agree with me that all this seems to be very chaotic. Trucks arrive from somewhere and they stand parked there for a fortnight. What I see here is an absence of organisation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. People arrived with old vehicles. There was even a truck which managed to reach base, and our mechanics gave it an overhaul, which lasted for three days. Those were the kind of vehicles that were used, so really -- but on the other hand, I was given a task -- well, first of all, I don't know about this. I'm -- I wasn't an expert with this kind of job. I had an insufficient number of men. So from the very first moment it appeared to be -- well, I don't know how to describe it, but I've never seen anything organised in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else now. As far as I can understand, it

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K88 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need now to go back into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The next witness, Your Honour, was scheduled to be Ambassador Kickert. I think the court was informed before, but if not, I have to advise that Ambassador Kickert has contacted us to indicate that he has had an inescapable appointment involving the Secretary-General of the United Nations and therefore is unable to attend as scheduled and has to be rescheduled. The information is that the commitment was sudden, but inescapable, as I indicated. The circumstance is we are unable to put on a witness for the rest of the week; however, we will have a full week based on the scheduling of the witnesses next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One thing we could do is address the issue of Mr. Coo, but it may be that it's felt there isn't adequate preparation time so far for that. Is it an issue that can be addressed today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid not, Your Honour, because it was actually a task of Mr. O'Sullivan and he's not present, as you can see, today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it something we could address tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, depends, Your Honour, if we would receive all the material, the disclosure from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We were told you were getting it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, just a part of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You didn't get all of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, we just got the first part of it and actually in Serbian, which is not a problem for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me add to what my colleague Mr. Zecevic has said. We have received some materials from the Prosecution yesterday and some today on CDs, but the difficulty is that the material on CDs has not been translated into B/C/S, nor has the second part of Mr. Coo's report, which still has to be revised or redacted. So even if something were to be changed, we need to consult about military matters and we also need the translation of the remaining part. So I don't believe anything would change between today and tomorrow, even if Mr. O'Sullivan were to turn up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm concerned about dealing with the opposition, if there is any, to the evidence of the witness and dealing with the question of how his evidence might be approached. Now, I understood there were issues to be debated on that. Now, the translation's not necessarily required for that purpose and so far as disclosure -- additional disclosure is concerned, I don't think it's required for that purpose, Mr. Visnjic. And as I understand it, it's not planned to call him in the immediate future; that he's a much later witness. So it's important to distinguish the issues of time for preparation to cross-examine him and time to prepare to address the issue of whether there's opposition to any elements of his statement. And it's the latter I'm concerned about. Is that something that could be addressed tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours, as you may have observed, we usually organise ourselves so that only one person speaks on behalf of all the teams. Mr. O'Sullivan is not here today because he's preparing for precisely this. Mr. Stamp said that he has a full five days next week. The witnesses he has put forward, except for Mr. Petritsch, will certainly not take as long as envisaged. As for Dr. Bar [phoen] or whatever, I don't know, let's say Mr. K, I don't know what one can ask him anyway. So we will be finished very soon next week and then we can do this next week. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me add something else. To the best of my understanding, we have informed the OTP of the problems concerning disclosure as we see them, and we are awaiting their response. We have told them what we expect to be disclosed in connection with this witness, and the ball is now in their court. We are awaiting their response. On the one hand, as Mr. Hannis informed us yesterday, he needed time to check whether there was anything in the material that might correspond to one part of our request, and also he needed to take up a standpoint with respect to some of the materials we asked to be disclosed in connection with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stamp, you're being given a clear warning that you may be over-optimistic about filling next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've said a number of times now that one of the main difficulties is that you fail to schedule any spare witnesses, and no court in the world runs on the basis of the arrival absolutely on time of every protected witness. And I think it's a major deficiency in the way in which you've conducted this prosecution. We heard submissions last week about the future timetable of the case, and on two occasions in the course of this week, counsel were engaged in informal discussions with a representative of the Trial Chamber about that. And I can say that we were in the end of the day, in spite of our initial reservations, in the end, broadly sympathetic to the principal requests. So if these were negotiating positions set particularly high in anticipation of an inevitable reduction, then you could have been pleasantly surprised. But our approach was largely based, in our preliminary consideration of these issues, upon the idea that the Prosecution case will be completed in the week of the 19th of March. Now, is that still the projected timetable?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thereabouts, Your Honour, as was -- is clear from what was said by Mr. Fila just now. A lot depends on the time the Defence takes to ask its questions. But I think the -- approximately the 19th of March is still feasible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah -- well, but the reason it is important is that we had given an indication that there would be a two-week break at the beginning of April. And if we are going to be generous in the time allotted for the preparation of the Defence case, we are equally insistent that that depends to some extent on early submissions if there are any under Rule 98 bis. And for the avoidance of any doubt, we should make it clear that we anticipate hearing these submissions more or less immediately after the completion of the Prosecution case. We think that parties should know about the evidence that is against them and that the Prosecution should know what the evidence is in support of their case. So we had in mind allocating the week of the 26th of March to this. We don't, obviously, know at the moment just how extensive these submissions might be, but assuming the worst comes to the worst and there are lengthy submissions on this matter, if we were to allow two hours to each party, that would be a total of 12 hours, which the parties obviously can divide up according to the needs. There are some who plainly would have a far better argument than others at that stage. And we might have to allocate an equivalent time to the Prosecution, but hopefully not, but that could be fitted into a week, and that would allow us to complete that exercise before the break. And then we could I think, bearing in mind the existence of that break and summer recess, which can be advanced, we could be fairly generous. But if that timetable goes in the immediate future, then we'll have to review it because -- review the overall position significantly, because we cannot be seen nor would it be right for us to actually be doing nothing over a significant period of time. But if that timetable's maintained then we have to be occupied in dealing with the response to these submissions and there are other things we can then do in the intervening period as well as take advantage of your preparation time to have any necessary recess fitted in. So I hope that these matters will be borne in mind. We will be reluctant until the position is a bit clearer to say finally what the time available for preparation of the Defence and the 65 ter documents will be, but you can take it that you should now assume that the -- any 98 bis submission will be very shortly after the conclusion of the Prosecution evidence. I note just in passing, Mr. Stamp, that since the beginning of December and prior to the beginning of this week, we had lost roughly 44 to 45 hours of time, roughly two weeks in a period of about two months of practical court time, and that's another nine and a half hours gone in between today and tomorrow. So it's something that is causing us anxiety, and we do really feel that you owe it to the Trial Chamber, in view of the way we've been sympathetic and generous throughout to the requests of parties, you owe it to us now to change your approach to the summoning of witnesses here and you need to have witnesses in reserve so that we can make proper use of the time. We've, we think, been far too lenient with you on that issue. And if you do not change your practice, then it may be we will fix a date for completion of your case, because that's the only way that enforce the regime that we thought was a reasonable regime. So I hope you will take serious -- or take these remarks into serious consideration when you are allocating time for witnesses over the next, I think, four weeks, that would be to the end of the week of the 19th of March. Regrettably, we now have no option but to adjourn until Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: [The accused Milutinovic and Pavkovic not present]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 9.47 a.m.,
